title: ME02b: Seeing the System: Leadership Beyond the Mask
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon continues his serialized story of Maya, a regional leader disillusioned with leadership development, by turning from the self and the virtues to the role and the system. Mintzberg's observations of executives' fragmented days validate her sense of chaos, while Goffman's account of everyday performance lets her see her shifting behavior as adaptation rather than inauthenticity. Gareth Morgan's eight organizational metaphors, from machine to psychic prison, become lenses for diagnosing which logic is operating in a given moment and for noticing how systems offload care and burnout onto individual leaders. Claydon's argument is that leadership is the carrying of simultaneous tensions inside constraint, and that self-blame is a misreading of structural contradiction. The essay ends with reflection prompts on self, role and system and a segue into adult development theory. It is a narrative-driven essay in leadership thinking aimed at managers who feel overloaded by contradictory demands.
points: Mintzberg's minute-by-minute study of executives is used to show that leadership is patterned chaos, not a tidy sequence of strategic acts.
Goffman's role-performance framing reframes adjusting to audiences as responsiveness instead of inauthenticity.
Morgan's eight metaphors are offered as a diagnostic toolkit, so a leader can name the logic in play instead of blaming herself.
The essay argues that organizations often reframe burnout as a resilience gap and push care onto leaders while leaving the system unchanged.
Leadership is defined as carrying tensions (delivering, aligning, growing, navigating) rather than embodying a fixed set of traits.
quotes: He didn’t offer a heroic model wrapped in illusion. He had bothered to observe real executives and tracked their days minute by minute. Strategy at 10:03. Culture at 10:12. Budget firefight by 10:21.
Goffman didn’t tell people who to be. He showed how we all perform, adaptively, in social roles. Not because we’re fake. But because we’re responsive.
Morgan’s thesis was simple: organisations are not machines or charts. They are systems of meaning. And the metaphors we use shape what we see and what we miss.
The organisation not as structure but as story. The trap wasn’t just outside. It was in her head.
She wasn’t just operating in a system. She was helping reinforce it. Not by malice, but by sincerity.
It’s where Maya stops pretending that there’s a perfect version of herself waiting to be unlocked. And begins learning how to lead inside the mess, without losing herself.
